a: The Philistines fought Israel.
t: The story begins with a death
p: After nine chapters of family lists, Chronicles starts its story at the end of Saul's life.
b: Chronicles skips everything from Adam to Saul's last battle except names: no Moses, no Joshua, no judges, no Samuel's rise. Its narrative opens on Mount Gilboa, and this chapter is copied from 1 Samuel 31 almost word for word. The few changes are the clues. Chronicles shortens the burial, moves Saul's head to Dagon's temple, says his whole house died, and then adds two verses of its own (10:13–14) to explain why he died. Saul is not the subject of the book; he is the dark background for David. Most scholars think the Chronicler expected readers to know Samuel already (Japhet, Williamson).

a: His whole house died, all together.
p: Samuel says Saul died with his armor-bearer and all his men. Chronicles says his whole house died.
b: The change is small in Hebrew and large in meaning. "House" can mean a family, but in the books of kings it usually means a royal line. Saul's family did not literally die out: his son Ish-bosheth (called Eshbaal in 8:33 and 9:39) reigned for two years (2 Samuel 2:8–10), and Jonathan's son Mephibosheth lived at David's table. Chronicles knows those names but tells none of those stories. Most interpreters take the verse as a verdict, not a census: on Gilboa Saul's dynasty ended, and the kingdom passed straight to David (10:14). There is no rival king in Chronicles and no civil war.

a: who were in the valley
p: Samuel speaks of Israelites beyond the valley and beyond the Jordan. Chronicles speaks only of those in the valley.
b: The valley is the Jezreel Valley, the broad plain at the foot of Mount Gilboa. In 1 Samuel 31:7 the panic spreads across the valley and even across the Jordan. Chronicles gives a shorter text, and some scholars think its Samuel scroll read differently here. The result is a smaller picture of the disaster: the towns of the valley are lost, but the Philistines do not take over half the country.

a: his skull they fastened up in the house of Dagon
p: Samuel says Saul's body hung on the wall of Beth-shan. Chronicles says his skull was fixed in Dagon's temple.
b: The two accounts can both be true: the body on a city wall, the head as a trophy in a temple. Chronicles never mentions Beth-shan or the goddesses called Ashtaroth; it names Dagon, the god whose statue once fell headless before the ark (1 Samuel 5:4). The word for skull, gulgolet, is the word behind "Golgotha," the Place of the Skull (Matthew 27:33). David had carried Goliath's head to Jerusalem (1 Samuel 17:54); now a Philistine temple holds the head of Israel's king.

a: They buried their bones beneath the oak in Jabesh.
p: Chronicles leaves out the night march to Beth-shan and the burning of the bodies, and the tree is an oak.
b: In Samuel the men of Jabesh walk all night, take the bodies down from the wall of Beth-shan, burn them and then bury the bones under a tamarisk. Chronicles has only the burial. Since it never put the bodies on the wall (10:10), there is nothing to take down. Many scholars also think the burning, rare and strange in Israel, was dropped as unfitting. The tree is an elah, a large tree such as an oak or terebinth, not Samuel's eshel, a tamarisk. Both words name a well-known tree in Jabesh, and either may be the older form of the story.

a: for his unfaithfulness
p: Chronicles' own verdict on Saul uses its strongest word for sin, the one it uses for the exile.
b: Ma'al means breaking faith with God, taking what belongs to him. Leviticus uses it for misusing holy things, and Joshua for Achan's theft of what was under the ban. Chronicles uses the word at its most important turning points: Judah went into exile for its unfaithfulness (9:1), and the last kings and priests were unfaithful until there was no cure (2 Chronicles 36:14–16). Saul's fall at the start of the story foreshadows Judah's fall at the end. The lesson for returned exiles is plain: kingdoms are lost by unfaithfulness and kept by seeking the LORD.
orig: בְּמַעֲלוֹ אֲשֶׁר מָעַל (bema'alo asher ma'al), 'in his unfaithfulness that he was unfaithful'

a: He had not kept the LORD's word
p: Chronicles does not say, but readers of Samuel know two failures: Gilgal and Amalek.
b: Samuel tells how Saul offered the sacrifice at Gilgal without waiting for Samuel (1 Samuel 13:8–14), and how he spared Agag and the best of the Amalekite herds against the LORD's command (1 Samuel 15). In both, Samuel says Saul did not keep what the LORD commanded, and that the kingdom will go to another man. Chronicles assumes the reader knows these stories and gives only the summary.

a: gone to a ghost of the dead to ask for answers
p: This is the night at Endor, when Saul had a woman call up the dead Samuel.
b: The Hebrew is lish'ol ba'ov lidrosh, "to ask of a ghost, to seek." An ov is the spirit of a dead person, or the person who calls it up (Leviticus 19:31; Deuteronomy 18:11). The verse uses both of Chronicles' words for consulting: sha'al, "ask," and darash, "seek." Saul is the king who sought the wrong source. The story is in 1 Samuel 28.

a: He did not ask the LORD.
t: But Saul did ask the LORD
p: 1 Samuel 28:6 says Saul asked the LORD and got no answer. How can Chronicles say he did not?
b: Interpreters have given several answers. (1) The verb here is darash, "seek," which in Chronicles means wholehearted turning to God (2 Chronicles 7:14; 2 Chronicles 15:12), not a single question. Saul asked once in panic; he never sought the LORD. (2) Some Jewish and Christian readers say his asking was worthless because he had already killed the priests of Nob (1 Samuel 22) and rejected the prophet's word. (3) Critical scholars see the Chronicler's sharp style of verdict: a king who seeks the LORD prospers, and one who does not falls. Chronicles does not deny 1 Samuel 28; it judges Saul's whole reign by its central word.

a: The LORD killed him
t: Saul killed himself, and the LORD killed him
p: Chronicles has just told how Saul fell on his own sword. Now it says the LORD put him to death.
b: Both statements stand side by side. The Bible often names God as the one behind events carried out by people (compare 2 Samuel 24:1 with 1 Chronicles 21:1). Here the point is a judgment: Saul's death was not bad luck in battle but the LORD's verdict on an unfaithful king. Jewish and Christian readers have generally seen this as God's providence working through human choices, not as a denial that Saul chose his own death. Some modern readers find the double description troubling, especially for questions of suicide; the text itself makes no comment on that act.

a: handed the kingship over to David, Jesse's son
p: The verb sabab, "turn," returns when the tribes come to Hebron "to hand Saul's kingdom over" to David (12:23).
b: Samuel had told Saul that the LORD had torn the kingdom from him and given it to a neighbor better than he (1 Samuel 15:28). Chronicles compresses years of struggle into one sentence: God turned the kingdom over. In 12:23 the same verb is used of the army's act at Hebron, so heaven's decision and the people's choice line up. Notice too that it is "the kingship" (melukhah), a word Chronicles prefers for a kingdom that belongs to God (17:14; 29:11).

a: All Israel gathered to David at Hebron.
p: In Samuel, David rules only Judah at Hebron for seven years. In Chronicles, all Israel comes at once.
b: 2 Samuel 1–4 tells of David's lament, his years as king of Judah alone, the war with Saul's house, Abner's murder and Ish-bosheth's assassination. Chronicles leaves all of it out (it mentions the seven years only in 3:4 and 29:27). The effect is a united people choosing David without a fight. "All Israel" is one of the book's favorite phrases; it appears in this chapter three times (11:1, 4, 10). Some see an idealized picture; others note that Chronicles is not hiding the facts, since its readers had Samuel, but telling the story of the kingdom from God's choice to the Temple.

a: This was what the LORD had said through Samuel.
p: Chronicles adds a line that ties the coronation to Samuel's secret anointing of the boy David.
b: Samuel anointed David in Bethlehem (1 Samuel 16:1–13) long before the elders anointed him at Hebron. Chronicles, which tells nothing of Samuel's life, makes sure the reader knows that the people's choice fulfilled the prophet's word. Elsewhere Chronicles names Samuel only in lists and as a source (6:28; 9:22; 26:28; 29:29).

a: they anointed him as king over Israel
p: Samuel follows the anointing with David's age and the length of his reign. Chronicles does not.
b: 2 Samuel 5:4–5 gives David's age (thirty) and his years in Hebron and Jerusalem. Chronicles moves that information to the end of his life (29:27). Interestingly, the Dead Sea scroll 4QSam-a, a copy of Samuel from about 50–25 BC, also lacks those two verses (see the variant at 2 Samuel 5:4–5). So Chronicles may not have cut them; its copy of Samuel may never have had them here.

a: that is, Jebus
p: The Bible sometimes calls Jerusalem Jebus, after the Jebusites who held it.
b: Joshua and Judges use the name Jebus (Joshua 15:8; Joshua 18:28; Judges 19:10–11). Outside the Bible, though, the city is called Jerusalem (Urusalim) as early as the Amarna letters of the 1300s BC, written by its king Abdi-Heba to Pharaoh. Most historians think "Jebus" was a biblical way of naming the city after its people rather than the name the city used itself. Chronicles adds the gloss for readers who knew only the later name.

a: You will not come in here.
t: The blind and the lame left out
p: Chronicles drops the puzzling saying about the blind and the lame and the water shaft.
b: In 2 Samuel 5:6–8 the Jebusites boast that even the blind and lame could hold off David, and David speaks of striking them through the water shaft. The passage is one of the hardest in Samuel. Chronicles keeps the boast but drops the rest and adds instead how Joab became commander (11:6). Scholars suggest it found the saying obscure, or unworthy of David, or simply irrelevant to its point: the city fell, and it became the City of David.

a: Joab son of Zeruiah was the first one up
p: Samuel never says how Joab got his post. Chronicles tells it here.
b: In Samuel Joab is simply the army commander (2 Samuel 8:16). Chronicles explains that he won the post by leading the attack on Jerusalem. "Went up" may echo the water shaft of 2 Samuel 5:8. For a long time visitors were shown "Warren's Shaft" in the City of David as the route, but excavations by Ronny Reich and Eli Shukron in the 1990s suggested that the shaft was not reachable in David's day; how the city fell is still debated. Chronicles shows no interest in the method, only in the man.

a: Joab brought the rest of the city back to life
p: The Hebrew verb is "make live." Used of a city, it means rebuilding what was ruined.
b: The verb chayah in this form usually means "keep alive" or "revive." Of stones and walls it means restoring them. The same use appears when Nehemiah's enemies mock the builders: will they bring the stones back to life from the heaps of rubble? (Nehemiah 4:2). Chronicles' readers, who were rebuilding Jerusalem themselves, would have heard the word gladly. Samuel does not mention Joab's work at all.

a: the LORD of Armies
p: The first time 1 Chronicles uses the title YHWH tseva'ot, "the LORD of Armies."
b: The Hebrew tseva'ot means "armies" or "hosts." The armies may be Israel's troops (1 Samuel 17:45), the angels, or the stars, and many think the title gathered all three meanings. Older English Bibles say "the LORD of hosts." This site renders it "the LORD of Armies" in every book. Chronicles uses the title only a few times (11:9; 17:7, 24), all in passages copied from Samuel.

a: These are the chiefs of David's warriors.
t: The heroes moved to the front
p: Samuel lists David's warriors near the end of his reign. Chronicles puts them at the start.
b: In Samuel the list of the Three and the Thirty sits in the appendix (2 Samuel 23:8–39). Chronicles moves it here and adds a sentence of its own: these men, with all Israel, made David king. The heroes become part of the people's choice, and the list grows into the long account of David's supporters in chapter 12. The list itself is copied closely, but with many small differences, most of them copying errors in one book or the other.

a: Jashobeam son of Hachmoni
p: Samuel calls him Josheb-basshebeth the Tahchemonite. Chronicles calls him Jashobeam son of Hachmoni.
b: Samuel's form, "he who sits in the seat," is probably a corruption. Greek manuscripts of Samuel point to a name like Ishbaal, "man of Baal" or "the Lord exists" (see the variant at 2 Samuel 23:8). Many scholars think the hero's real name was Ishbaal, and that scribes, uneasy with "Baal," changed it in different ways in the two books. A Jashobeam also leads the first army division in 27:2. "Son of Hachmoni" may mean "the Hachmonite," a clan name (compare 27:32).

a: He swung his spear over three hundred
p: Chronicles' wording helped scholars repair a broken line in Samuel. Its number is smaller.
b: Samuel's Hebrew reads "He was Adino the Eznite; eight hundred fell at his hand." Chronicles has "he swung his spear over three hundred," and most scholars think Samuel's strange name hides the same words, 'orer et-chanito, "he swung his spear" (see the variant at 2 Samuel 23:8). The numbers differ. Since Abishai's feat is also three hundred (11:20), some think a copyist's eye carried that number up into Jashobeam's line; others think Samuel's eight hundred grew. There is no way to be sure.

a: at Pas-dammim
p: Where Samuel says "when they jeered at the Philistines," Chronicles has the place name Pas-dammim.
b: The two Hebrew phrases look alike: Samuel becharpam, "when they taunted," Chronicles bappas dammim, "at Pas-dammim." Pas-dammim is probably Ephes-dammim, "the edge of blood," where the Philistines camped before Goliath came out (1 Samuel 17:1). Most scholars prefer Chronicles here: it explains Samuel's vague "there" (2 Samuel 23:9).

a: A field there was planted thick with barley
p: Chronicles' copy lost part of the list here, so Eleazar gets the deed of another hero.
b: In 2 Samuel 23:9–12, Eleazar fights until his hand clings to his sword. Then a second hero, Shammah, holds a field of lentils at Lehi when the troops flee. Both stories contain the words "the Philistines gathered." A copyist's eye seems to have jumped from the first to the second, skipping the end of Eleazar's story and Shammah's name. So in Chronicles the field belongs to Eleazar, and the verbs in 11:14 become plural. That is also why Chronicles names only two of the Three. Copying slips of this kind, from one repeated phrase to the next, are common in all ancient manuscripts.

a: to the rock where David was
p: Chronicles reads "to the rock"; Samuel has "at harvest." The Hebrew words differ by one letter.
b: In Hebrew, el-hatstsur "to the rock" (Chronicles) and el-qatsir "at harvest" (Samuel) look much alike. Either fits: the cave of Adullam is in rocky hills, and the Philistines raided at harvest time. See the variant at 2 Samuel 23:13.

a: My God, I could never do this!
p: Chronicles often says "God" (Elohim) where Samuel says "the LORD" (YHWH).
b: Samuel reads "Far be it from me, LORD." Chronicles reads "Far be it from me, from my God." The same switch happens many times in these chapters: "the ark of God" (13:6, 12, 14), "David asked God" (14:10, 14), "God has burst through" (14:11). It is not a rule, since Chronicles uses YHWH freely too. Scholars think it reflects a later style that favored "God" in some phrases. Readers should not read much theology into each change.

a: Abshai
p: Chronicles spells Joab's brother Abshai every time. Samuel spells him Abishai.
b: The Hebrew of Chronicles has Avshai here and in 18:12, 19:11 and 19:15; Samuel has Avishai. It is the same man, Joab's brother and a son of Zeruiah (2:16). The Plain keeps the spelling of each book, as it does for other names that the two books spell differently. Most English versions use "Abishai" in both.

a: five cubits high
p: Chronicles gives the Egyptian's height and a spear like a weaver's beam. Samuel does not.
b: Five cubits is about seven and a half feet (2.3 meters). The spear "like a weaver's beam" is the phrase used of Goliath's spear (1 Samuel 17:7) and of the spear of Goliath's brother (20:5). So Benaiah, who fights a giant with only a stick, becomes a small copy of David with his sling. Some scholars think Chronicles' copy of Samuel had these details; others think the Chronicler added them, borrowing the Goliath language. Either way the giant-killing theme ties the hero list to David's own story.

a: The warriors of the army were
p: About a dozen names in this list are spelled differently in Samuel. Most are copying errors.
b: Compare the two lists and the differences jump out: Shammoth for Shammah, Heled for Heleb, Hurai for Hiddai, Abiel for Abi-albon, Hashem for Jashen, Sachar for Sharar. Many come from letters that look alike in Hebrew script, such as d and r, or b and m. Neither book is always the better copy. Scholars rebuild the list by comparing both with the Greek. For a reader, the lesson is the honesty of the record: the Bible came down through copyists, and the copies can be compared.

a: Shammoth the Harorite; Helez the Pelonite;
p: Samuel lists Elika the Harodite between Shammah and Helez. Chronicles does not.
b: In 2 Samuel 23:25 two men in a row are "the Harodite." A copyist could easily jump from the first to the second and drop the name between. "Harorite" for "Harodite" is the confusion of d and r, which look nearly the same in Hebrew writing. Harod was a spring below Mount Gilboa (Judges 7:1).

a: Sibbecai the Hushathite
p: Samuel's list has Mebunnai; Chronicles has Sibbecai, the hero who kills a giant in 20:4.
b: Sibbecai the Hushathite appears again in 20:4 (also in 2 Samuel 21:18) and as a division commander in 27:11. In Hebrew script the two names share several letters, and most scholars think Chronicles has the right one here and Samuel's "Mebunnai" is a copying error.

a: Ithai son of Ribai
p: Samuel's list calls him Ittai. Chronicles spells the name Ithai.
b: 2 Samuel 23:29 has Ittai, Chronicles Itai (KJV "Ithai"). This Benjaminite from Gibeah, Saul's hometown, is not Ittai the Gittite, the Philistine who stayed loyal to David (2 Samuel 15:19–22).

a: Ahijah the Pelonite
p: Samuel lists Eliam son of Ahithophel. Bathsheba's father may have been an Eliam. Chronicles lacks him.
b: In 2 Samuel 23:34 the list has "Eliam son of Ahithophel the Gilonite," and 2 Samuel 11:3 names Bathsheba as daughter of an Eliam. Chronicles has "Hepher the Mecherathite; Ahijah the Pelonite" in about the same place. Was the name removed to keep Bathsheba out of the book? Most scholars think not: the whole stretch of the list is damaged in both books, "Mecherathite" seems to come from Samuel's "Maacathite," and Chronicles keeps Uriah the Hittite in plain view (11:41). The difference is best seen as a scribal one.

a: Mibhar son of Hagri
p: Samuel reads "from Zobah; Bani the Gadite." Chronicles' name grew from the same letters.
b: Write Samuel's mitstsovah bani haggadi without vowels and set it beside Chronicles' mivchar ben-hagri: most of the consonants match. One of the two is a misreading of the other, and most scholars think Samuel's is the original.

a: Uriah the Hittite
p: Chronicles never tells the story of Bathsheba and Uriah, but it keeps Uriah's name.
b: In Samuel this list ends with Uriah, the loyal soldier David had killed so he could keep his wife (2 Samuel 11). Chronicles leaves out that whole story (see 20:1). Readers have explained the silence in three main ways. (1) Idealizing: Chronicles polishes David into a model king, as Julius Wellhausen argued. (2) Assumed knowledge: its readers knew Samuel, and Chronicles tells only what serves its theme; leaving Uriah's name in the list shows it was not hiding anything. (3) Theology of the Temple builder: the book follows David's public work for the ark and the Temple, and it does include his great sin of the census (chapter 21), because that sin leads to the Temple site.

a: Zabad son of Ahlai
p: Samuel's list ends with Uriah. Chronicles adds sixteen more names from another source.
b: From Zabad on (11:41b–47) the names are not in Samuel. Several come from east of the Jordan: Reubenites (11:42), men of Ashtaroth and Aroer (11:44), even a Moabite (11:46). Scholars think the Chronicler had a further list of David's warriors, perhaps once part of the same roll. An Ahlai appears in the genealogy of Judah (2:31, 34), but whether this is the same family is unknown.

a: Ithmah the Moabite
p: A Moabite, an Ammonite (11:39) and a Hittite (11:41) serve among David's warriors.
b: Moab and Ammon were barred from the LORD's assembly in Deuteronomy 23:3, yet both appear among David's warriors, and David's own great-grandmother Ruth was a Moabite. Chronicles, written when marriages with foreigners were hotly debated (Ezra 9–10; Nehemiah 13:23–27), keeps these names without comment.

a: These are the men who came to David at Ziklag
p: Chapter 12 is not in Samuel. It lists the men who joined David before and after Saul's death.
b: The chapter runs backward in time and then forward: Ziklag, where David lived among the Philistines (1 Samuel 27), the fortress in the wilderness (12:8, 16), the Philistine march against Saul (12:19), then the great gathering at Hebron (12:23–40). Its message is that men from every tribe, even Saul's own, were turning to David while Saul was still alive. Some scholars think the Chronicler drew on old military lists; others see a picture built to show all Israel behind David. Many hold a middle view: old names, framed by the Chronicler's theme.

a: shut out by Saul
p: The Hebrew 'atsur means held back or shut in. Here it describes David's life as a fugitive.
b: Translators read the phrase in different ways: David was "banished from Saul's presence," "kept from moving freely because of Saul," or "still in hiding from Saul." All agree on the setting: David's years as an outlaw, when he lived at Ziklag under the Philistine king Achish.

a: with the right hand or the left
p: Benjaminites were known for fighting left-handed. These men could use either hand.
b: Ehud the Benjaminite killed the king of Moab with his left hand (Judges 3:15–21), and Judges 20:16 tells of seven hundred picked Benjaminite slingers. The tribe's name means "son of the right hand," which makes the fame of its left-handers a small irony. Being able to throw with either hand let a slinger or archer shoot from any side of a wall or a rock.

a: They came from Saul's own kin in Benjamin.
p: The first men named as David's supporters are Saul's relatives.
b: Chronicles begins the roll with Benjamin, Saul's tribe, and repeats the point at Hebron (12:29). Even Saul's kinsmen, it says, saw that the future lay with David. In Samuel, Benjaminite loyalty to Saul's house runs much deeper, and Shimei curses David as late as Absalom's revolt (2 Samuel 16:5–8). Chronicles chooses to remember those who came over.

a: a warrior among the Thirty and over the Thirty
p: Ishmaiah is not on Samuel's list of the Thirty. The note shows how loose the term had become.
b: "The Thirty" seems to have been an honor group rather than an exact count; Samuel's list reaches thirty-seven (2 Samuel 23:39). Ishmaiah, from Gibeon, is otherwise unknown. In Hebrew Bibles the second half of this verse is counted as verse 5, so the Hebrew chapter has 41 verses; this site follows the English numbering.

a: the Korahites
p: Korahites are best known as Levite singers. These men are listed among Benjaminites.
b: The sons of Korah were a Levite family of gatekeepers and singers (9:19; Psalm 42–49 titles). A Korahite in a list of Benjaminites is surprising. Some scholars think this is a different clan of the same name, from Benjamin or Judah (compare the Korah of 2:43). Others think Levites living in Benjamin's towns joined David with their neighbors.

a: They had lion faces, and they could run like gazelles
p: Ancient war poetry praised heroes as fierce as lions and as quick as gazelles.
b: David's lament praised Saul and Jonathan as swifter than eagles and stronger than lions (2 Samuel 1:23). Asahel ran like a gazelle (2 Samuel 2:18). Moses' blessing pictures Gad crouching like a lion (Deuteronomy 33:20). The Gadites lived east of the Jordan, so to reach David in the Judean wilderness they had to cross the river and the hill country.

a: Even the smallest of them was worth a hundred
t: Worth a hundred, or over a hundred?
p: The Hebrew can mean each man was a match for a hundred, or that each commanded at least a hundred.
b: Word for word it reads "one to a hundred, the small, and the great to a thousand." Many modern translations hear a boast of strength, like Leviticus 26:8 (five chase a hundred) and Deuteronomy 32:30 (one chases a thousand). The King James Version reads it as rank: the least was over a hundred men, the greatest over a thousand. Both fit "heads of the army."
orig: אֶחָד לְמֵאָה הַקָּטָן וְהַגָּדוֹל לְאָלֶף (echad leme'ah haqqatan vehaggadol le'alef)

a: in the first month, when the river was over all its banks
p: The first month, Nisan, falls in March or April, when the Jordan runs high.
b: Spring rains and snowmelt from Mount Hermon once swelled the Jordan beyond its banks at harvest time (Joshua 3:15). Crossing it then was dangerous. The detail echoes Israel's crossing under Joshua, and it makes the Gadites heroes before they even reach David.

a: the Spirit put Amasai
t: The Spirit puts on a man
p: The Spirit "clothed itself" with Amasai, the same rare picture used of Gideon.
b: The verb is lavash, "put on clothing." The Spirit wears the man like a garment (Judges 6:34; 2 Chronicles 24:20). In Gideon's story the Spirit brings courage for battle; here it brings speech, a short inspired poem. Chronicles often has the Spirit come on people who are not called prophets, to speak a word for the moment (2 Chronicles 15:1; 2 Chronicles 20:14). The Hebrew says only ruach, "spirit," without "of God" or "of the LORD" as in Judges 6:34; capital-S "Spirit" is the usual reading, and the Aramaic Targum of Chronicles expands the line to make its divine source plain. Some scholars think Amasai is Amasa, later Absalom's commander (2 Samuel 17:25), but the link is uncertain.

a: Yours, David!
t: The answer to a rebel's cry
p: Amasai's words reverse the rebels' cry "no share in David, no inheritance in the son of Jesse."
b: Twice in Israel's history the northern tribes walked away from David's house with a slogan naming David and the son of Jesse: under Sheba (2 Samuel 20:1) and under Jeroboam (1 Kings 12:16). Amasai's oath uses the same pair of names to say the opposite: we belong to David, we stand with Jesse's son. For readers in Chronicles' day, when the north and south were long divided, it was a picture of what loyalty to David's house could look like.

a: when he came with the Philistines for the battle with Saul
p: Chronicles keeps an awkward fact from Samuel: David marched with the Philistines against Saul.
b: In 1 Samuel 29 David and his men march with Achish of Gath toward Saul's last battle, and the Philistine lords send them home because they do not trust them. Chronicles adds that the men of Manasseh came over to David at that moment, and it stresses that David's men did not help the Philistines. The rulers' fear, "our heads will pay for it," echoes 1 Samuel 29:4.

a: against the raiding band
p: Probably the Amalekites who burned Ziklag while David was away.
b: When David came back from the Philistine camp he found Ziklag burned and the families taken. He chased the raiders and won them all back (1 Samuel 30). The word gedud, "raiding band," is used there (1 Samuel 30:8, 15). Chronicles names the Manassite commanders who helped in that chase.

a: like the camp of God
p: A Hebrew way of saying "an enormous camp," with a hint of the heavenly army.
b: Hebrew sometimes adds "of God" to mean "very great" ("a mighty prince," literally "a prince of God," Genesis 23:6). But the phrase also recalls Jacob's vision of angels at Mahanaim, which he named "God's camp" (Genesis 32:1–2). Both senses may be meant: David's army grows until it looks like heaven's.

a: Here are the counts
p: The numbers in 12:24–37 add up to more than 340,000 men. How should we read them?
b: Readers take three approaches. (1) Literal: the whole fighting strength of the tribes came. (2) Units: the Hebrew elef, "thousand," can also mean a clan or a military unit (Judges 6:15), so the totals may count units, not men; this view was argued by George Mendenhall and others. (3) Ideal: the Chronicler uses large round figures to say that all Israel came, as at Sinai. One detail argues against simple flattery of Judah: Judah sends one of the smallest groups (6,800), while far tribes such as Zebulun (50,000) and Asher (40,000) send many more.

a: Jehoiada was leader of Aaron's family
p: Probably the father of Benaiah, the hero of 11:22. 27:5 calls Benaiah son of Jehoiada "the priest."
b: Chronicles counts priests and Levites among the fighting men who came to Hebron. Jehoiada here is "the leader of Aaron," that is, of the priestly family. If he is Benaiah's father, David's famous guard captain came from a priestly house. The title does not mean high priest; Chronicles does not name one for this time.

a: Zadok, a young man and a strong warrior
p: Chronicles has Zadok at Hebron from the start, long before Samuel mentions him.
b: In Samuel, Zadok suddenly appears as priest in 2 Samuel 8:17. Chronicles gives him a priestly family tree (6:8, 53) and here shows him as a young fighter who joined David at Hebron with his clan. For Chronicles, whose Temple priests were "sons of Zadok," it mattered that their ancestor had stood with David from the beginning.
r: 2 Samuel 8:17; 1 Chronicles 6:8; 1 Chronicles 6:53; 1 Chronicles 15:11; 1 Chronicles 16:39; Ezekiel 44:15

a: men who knew how to read the times
p: One of Chronicles' best-known lines. Jewish tradition took it to mean skill in the calendar and the law.
b: The Hebrew says they "knew understanding for the times, to know what Israel should do." The plain sense is political wisdom: they saw that the moment had come to back David. Jewish tradition read more into it: the Aramaic Targum of Chronicles speaks of men skilled in fixing the new moons and the calendar, and Rashi (on Genesis 49:15) links Issachar's two hundred chiefs to the heads of the great law court. Christians today often quote the verse as a call for leaders who understand their own age.

a: with no divided heart
p: A Hebrew idiom: a double heart is a two-faced one.
b: The Hebrew is belo lev valev, "without a heart and a heart." Psalm 12:2 uses "a heart and a heart" for flatterers who say one thing and mean another. Zebulun's men had only one heart, set on David. The book's matching phrase comes in 12:38: "with a whole heart."

a: ready to keep rank
p: The Hebrew says Zebulun's men could "keep rank." The Greek says they came "to help."
b: The Leningrad Codex has vela'ador, "and to keep rank" (KJV "which could keep rank"), from the same root as "take their places in the battle line" in 12:38. The Greek has boethesai, "to help," which implies the Hebrew la'azor, a difference of one letter, and many modern versions follow it. The Plain keeps the Hebrew.

a: with a whole heart
p: A favorite phrase of Chronicles: undivided, complete loyalty.
b: Lev shalem means a heart that is whole, at peace, entire. David will ask the same of Solomon (28:9; 29:19), and the people give gifts for the Temple with a whole heart (29:9). The word shalem is related to shalom, "peace," and to the name Solomon.

a: Israel was full of joy.
p: Joy, simchah, marks every great gathering in Chronicles.
b: The coronation ends with three days of eating and drinking, supplied from as far north as Naphtali. Chronicles likes to end its great scenes with joy: the ark's arrival (15:16, 25), the gifts for the Temple (29:9, 22), Hezekiah's Passover (2 Chronicles 30:26). The picture is of a people united around David, and later around worship in Jerusalem.

a: David talked it over with the commanders
p: Chronicles tells the ark story before David's palace and his Philistine wars. Samuel tells it after.
b: In 2 Samuel 5–6 the order is: Jerusalem taken, Hiram builds David a palace, David's sons, two Philistine wars, then the ark. Chronicles moves the first attempt to bring the ark (2 Samuel 6:1–11) ahead of all that. So the new king's first act after taking his city is to consult the people about the ark. The three months the ark waits at Obed-edom's house (13:14) are then filled with blessing on David: a palace, sons and victories (chapter 14). Scholars agree the change is deliberate, and that it puts worship at the center of David's reign.

a: let us send word out everywhere
p: The verb behind "send out everywhere" is parats, "break out."
b: Literally David says "let us break out, let us send." Here the verb means to spread out or act at once and widely: the call is to go out to every corner of Israel. The same root returns in 13:11, 14:11 and 15:13; see the chapter page for how commentators read the repetition.
orig: נִפְרְצָה נִשְׁלְחָה (nifretsah nishlechah), 'let us break out, let us send'

a: the priests and the Levites in their towns with pasturelands
p: The Levites had no tribal territory. They lived in towns given them across Israel, with fields around them.
b: The law assigned forty-eight towns to the Levites, each with open land around it for their flocks (Numbers 35:1–8; Joshua 21). Chronicles lists them in 6:54–81. David's call reaches them first, because the ark is their charge. The word migrash, "pastureland," is the open strip around a town.

a: In the days of Saul we did not seek it.
p: Seeking God is the great theme of Chronicles. Saul did not seek; David does.
b: Darash means to look for, consult, turn to. Saul died because he "did not ask the LORD" (10:14, the same verb). David's first proposal is to seek the ark. The theme runs through the book: "Seek the LORD and his strength" (16:11), and the famous promise to Solomon that if God's people seek his face he will heal their land (2 Chronicles 7:14). The ark had stayed in Kiriath-jearim for twenty years and more (1 Samuel 7:1–2), almost forgotten.
orig: לֹא דְרַשְׁנֻהוּ (lo derashnuhu), 'we did not seek it'

a: from Shihor in Egypt to Lebo-hamath
p: The ideal borders of the land, from Egypt's edge in the south to Lebo-hamath in the north.
b: Shihor is either an eastern branch of the Nile or the Wadi el-Arish, the "Brook of Egypt" (Joshua 13:3; Isaiah 23:3). Lebo-hamath, "the entrance to Hamath," lay in the Beqaa Valley of Lebanon, the northern limit promised in Numbers 34:8. Samuel speaks of thirty thousand picked men (2 Samuel 6:1); Chronicles calls the whole people from border to border. Solomon's dedication of the Temple will gather Israel from the same two ends (2 Chronicles 7:8).

a: to Baalah, to Kiriath-jearim in Judah
p: Chronicles names the town Baalah and explains it as Kiriath-jearim. The scroll 4QSam-a agrees.
b: The Masoretic text of 2 Samuel 6:2 reads "from Baale-judah," as if David set out from there. Chronicles reads "to Baalah, to Kiriath-jearim," and the Dead Sea scroll 4QSam-a has a similar text. This site's 2 Samuel follows the scroll and Chronicles (see the variant there). Joshua 15:9 gives the same old name: "Baalah, that is, Kiriath-jearim." Here Chronicles preserves a better Samuel text than the Masoretic one.

a: onto a new cart
p: A new cart was how the Philistines sent the ark home. The law said it must be carried on poles.
b: When the Philistines returned the ark, they put it on a new cart drawn by cows (1 Samuel 6:7). David's men copy them. But the law said the Kohathite Levites were to carry the holy things on their shoulders with poles (Exodus 25:14; Numbers 4:15; Numbers 7:9). Samuel does not point this out. Chronicles will, after the disaster: "we did not seek him the way the ruling requires" (15:13).
r: 1 Samuel 6:7–12; Exodus 25:12–15; Numbers 4:15; Numbers 7:9; 1 Chronicles 15:2; 1 Chronicles 15:13

a: because the oxen stumbled
p: The verb shamat may mean the oxen stumbled, or that they let the cart slip.
b: Shamat elsewhere means "let drop" or "release" (as in the year of release, Deuteronomy 15:2). Here it may mean the oxen stumbled, or that they jolted the cart and let the ark tip.

a: he struck him for putting his hand out to the ark
p: Uzzah meant to help. Readers have asked for three thousand years why he was struck down.
b: The holiness reading: the law warned that even the Levites who carried the holy things "must not touch the holy things. If they do, they will die" (Numbers 4:15). God's holiness is not a thing to be steadied. Chronicles' own reading: the fault was the whole procession's, which did not seek the LORD "the way the ruling requires" (15:13). Jewish tradition: the Talmud (Sotah 35a) says David had forgotten the law of carrying, and Uzzah, who had lived with the ark, should have known it. Critical readers see an old story explaining the place name Perez-uzzah. Samuel's Hebrew says only "for the offense"; Chronicles states the reason plainly (see the variant at 2 Samuel 6:7).

a: Obed-edom the Gittite
p: A man from Gath took in the ark. Chronicles later lists an Obed-edom among the Levites.
b: "Gittite" usually means someone from Gath, the Philistine city that Ittai the Gittite also came from (2 Samuel 15:19). But there was also a Levite town Gath-rimmon (Joshua 21:24–25). Chronicles names an Obed-edom among the Levite gatekeepers and musicians (15:18, 21, 24; 16:38) and gives him a large blessed family (26:4–8). Some think there were two men; others think Chronicles counts the ark's host among the Levites. Either way, God's blessing on his house showed David that the ark was not a curse.

a: The LORD brought blessing on Obed-edom's family
p: Jewish tradition counted Obed-edom's blessing in children, from the list in 26:4–8.
b: 1 Chronicles 26:5 says of Obed-edom's eight sons, "for God had blessed him," and 26:8 counts sixty-two descendants. The Talmud (Berakhot 63b–64a) joins these passages and treats his house as a lesson: if the ark blessed the man who kept it for three months, how much more someone who welcomes a Torah scholar into his home and provides for him. In Chronicles' order, the blessing also spills over onto David in the next chapter.

a: king of Tyre
p: Hiram of Tyre was Solomon's partner for the Temple. Was he already king when David took Jerusalem?
b: Tyre's king lists, preserved by Josephus, suggest Hiram I reigned about 980–947 BC, which would place this embassy late in David's reign rather than just after the capture of Jerusalem. Both Samuel and Chronicles arrange these episodes by theme, not strict order. Chronicles places Hiram's help here, during the three months the ark waited, as the first sign of God's blessing on David's house.

a: In Jerusalem David took still more wives
p: Samuel says "wives and concubines." Chronicles says only wives.
b: Chronicles knows about David's concubines (3:9), so it is not hiding them. It may have trimmed the phrase as unimportant, or for modesty. Deuteronomy 17:17 warned that a king must not take many wives, and neither book comments on David's household. Chronicles' list of sons (14:4–7) is what it wants: the line that leads to Solomon.

a: Shammua, Shobab, Nathan, Solomon
p: Matthew traces Jesus through Solomon. Luke traces him through Nathan.
b: Matthew 1:6 follows David's line through Solomon and the kings of Judah. Luke 3:31 goes through Nathan, another son born in Jerusalem. Christians have explained the two lines as Joseph's and Mary's, or as legal and natural descent; Jewish tradition traces the Messiah through Solomon. Chronicles' list of David's sons is the Old Testament source behind both.

a: Elpelet
p: Chronicles names Elpelet and Nogah, who are not in Samuel's list.
b: Samuel lists eleven sons born in Jerusalem (2 Samuel 5:14–16); Chronicles, here and in 3:5–8, lists thirteen, with Elpelet and Nogah added and an Eliphelet at the end as well as Elpelet near the start. Some think two sons died young and dropped out of Samuel's list; others think a copyist doubled a name. The lists differ in spelling too.

a: Beeliada
p: Samuel and 3:8 call him Eliada, "God knows." Here the older name, with Baal, survives.
b: Baal means "lord" or "master," and in early Israel it could even be used of the LORD (Hosea 2:16). Later, when Baal meant only the Canaanite god, scribes often changed Baal names: Eshbaal became Ish-bosheth, "man of shame," and Merib-baal became Mephibosheth. Chronicles sometimes keeps the older forms (8:33–34; 9:39–40), and Beeliada looks like another one. So here Chronicles probably preserves the original name.

a: David asked God
p: Saul "did not ask the LORD" (10:14). David asks before each battle.
b: The verb sha'al, "ask," is the word used for asking God through the priest's ephod or the sacred lots (1 Samuel 23:2–4; 1 Samuel 30:7–8). Chronicles sets the two kings side by side: Saul asked a ghost and fell; David asks God and wins. The answer "I will put them in your power" comes twice, before both victories.

a: God has burst through my enemies by my hand
p: Isaiah remembers this battle as a sign that God can rise up against his own people too.
b: Isaiah warns Jerusalem that the LORD will rise up as at Mount Perazim and the valley at Gibeon, to do a strange deed (Isaiah 28:21). The prophet takes David's two victories, here and at Gibeon (14:16), and turns them around: the God who broke through Israel's enemies can break through Israel. On the root parats, see 13:2.

a: David gave the word, and they were burned in the fire.
p: Samuel says David and his men carried off the Philistine idols. Chronicles says they were burned.
b: Deuteronomy commands: "Burn the idols of their gods in the fire" (Deuteronomy 7:25; compare Deuteronomy 7:5). Samuel's "carried them off" (2 Samuel 5:21) might suggest that David kept the idols as trophies. Most scholars think Chronicles is making sure the reader knows David obeyed the law. Others suggest both happened: the idols were taken and then burned. The scene also reverses the old story in which the Philistines carried off Israel's ark (1 Samuel 5).

a: from Gibeon all the way to Gezer
p: The Philistines were driven from the hills down to the coastal plain.
b: Gibeon lay about six miles northwest of Jerusalem; Gezer guarded the road down to the coast. The route is the same one Joshua followed against the Amorite kings (Joshua 10:10–12). The Masoretic text of Samuel reads Geba, a town to the northeast; the Greek of Samuel agrees with Chronicles (see the variant at 2 Samuel 5:25).

a: the LORD laid the dread of him on every nation
t: The dread of the LORD's king
p: Chronicles adds this verse. The fear of God falls on Israel's enemies when Israel is faithful.
b: The phrase echoes the promise of the conquest: "I will begin to put the dread and fear of you on the peoples" (Deuteronomy 2:25). Chronicles uses it again for its faithful kings: Asa (2 Chronicles 14:14), Jehoshaphat (2 Chronicles 17:10; 2 Chronicles 20:29). It is the book's way of saying that the victories came from God, not from David's army alone.

a: set up a tent for it
p: David set up a new tent for the ark in Jerusalem. The old tabernacle stayed at Gibeon.
b: Chronicles alone says that the tabernacle Moses made, with its bronze altar, stood at the high place of Gibeon during David's reign (16:39; 21:29; 2 Chronicles 1:3–6). So for a generation Israel had two centers: the ark in David's tent in Jerusalem, with Levite singers, and the altar at Gibeon, with Zadok and the sacrifices. Solomon's Temple would bring them together. Historians debate whether this reflects an old memory or the Chronicler's way of explaining why Solomon worshiped at Gibeon (1 Kings 3:4).

a: The ark of God is not to be carried by anyone but the Levites
p: David now applies the law of Numbers 4. Only Levites may carry the ark.
b: Deuteronomy says the LORD set apart the tribe of Levi to carry the ark of the LORD's covenant (Deuteronomy 10:8). Numbers gives the task to the Kohathites, with poles on their shoulders (Numbers 4:15; Numbers 7:9). Chronicles shows David learning from the death of Uzzah: the first failure came from ignoring God's way of doing things. Samuel tells only that the second attempt succeeded (2 Samuel 6:12–13).

a: Aaron's descendants and the Levites
p: Chronicles always separates the priests, Aaron's sons, from the other Levites.
b: All priests were Levites, but not all Levites were priests. Only the descendants of Aaron offered sacrifice; the other Levites carried, guarded, sang and served (Numbers 3:5–10; Numbers 18:1–7). This two-level system is assumed throughout Chronicles and Ezra–Nehemiah, and it was the order of the Second Temple. Critical scholars think it took its final shape after the exile (compare Ezekiel 44:10–16); traditional readers trace it to Moses.

a: of Kohath's descendants
p: The three great Levite families, plus three Kohathite branches, send 862 men.
b: Levi had three sons, Kohath, Merari and Gershom (6:16). Elizaphan, Hebron and Uzziel were Kohathite branches (Exodus 6:18–22; Numbers 3:30). So four of the six groups here are Kohathites, the family given charge of the ark and the holy things (Numbers 4:4–15). The leaders' names reappear in 15:11.

a: Make yourselves holy
p: To consecrate oneself meant washing, clean clothes and keeping away from what made a person impure.
b: The verb hitqaddesh is used when Israel prepared to meet God at Sinai: wash clothes, stay away from sexual relations, be ready (Exodus 19:10–15). Priests and Levites did the same before handling holy things (2 Chronicles 29:5, 15). Chronicles stresses that this time every rule is kept.

a: we did not seek him the way the ruling requires
p: David blames the first failure on not following the law's procedure, the mishpat.
b: Mishpat is the word for a ruling or a prescribed way (this site renders it "ruling"). The Levites were to carry the ark as the law required, and they had not. David says "we": he does not blame Uzzah alone. Chronicles' word "seek" (see 13:3) and its word "burst out" (see 13:2) both return here, tying the explanation to the disaster.

a: on their shoulders, with the poles resting on them
p: The ark was built with rings and poles so that it could be carried without being touched.
b: Exodus 25:12–15 describes the gold rings at the ark's corners and the acacia poles that were never to be removed. The Kohathites carried it on their shoulders (Numbers 7:9). Chronicles says this was done "the way Moses had commanded, as the LORD had said," pointing back to those laws.

a: to appoint some of their kinsmen as singers
p: Chronicles credits David with organizing the Levite singers. Samuel and Kings say nothing of it.
b: Chronicles traces the Temple's music to David here and in chapters 16 and 25, and Ezra and Nehemiah agree (Ezra 3:10; Nehemiah 12:24, 45–46). Traditional readers accept this: David was a musician and psalm writer (1 Samuel 16:23; Amos 6:5). Many critical scholars think the singer families of the Second Temple, Asaph, Heman and Jeduthun, read their own order back into David's time, though they grant that Temple music was old. Some suggest the lists themselves grew over time (see 25:1–31).

a: Heman son of Joel
p: Asaph, Heman and Ethan are the singers named in the titles of several psalms.
b: Twelve psalms are "of Asaph" (50; 73–83). Psalm 88 is "of Heman the Ezrahite" and Psalm 89 "of Ethan the Ezrahite." Heman and Ethan the Ezrahites are also wise men in 1 Kings 4:31. In Chronicles they lead the three Levite families: Heman of Kohath, Asaph of Gershom, Ethan of Merari (6:33–47). In 16:41 and 25:1 Jeduthun stands where Ethan is here, and some think they are the same man.

a: Ben,
p: "Ben" means "son of." It is probably a copying slip, since the name is missing from the list in 15:20.
b: The same men are listed again with their instruments in 15:20, and Ben is not there. Many scholars think a scribe wrote "son of" and then lost the father's name, and many modern translations leave "Ben" out. The Plain keeps the Hebrew as it stands. Similarly, "Jaaziel" here is "Aziel" in 15:20 and perhaps "Jeiel" in 16:5.

a: set to alamoth
p: A music term of uncertain meaning, also in the title of Psalm 46.
b: 'Alamot looks like the plural of 'almah, "young woman." Many think it means a high register, "in the manner of young women's voices," for the lyres; others think it names a tune or an instrument. It appears in the heading of Psalm 46. The ancient translators already did not know it.

a: set to the sheminith, to lead
p: Sheminith means "the eighth." To lead, lenatseach, is the word behind "for the director" in the psalms.
b: Sheminit, "the eighth," may be a lower register (perhaps an octave below the alamoth), an eight-stringed instrument, or a tune. It is in the titles of Psalms 6 and 12. Lenatseach, "to lead" or "to direct," is the same word as lamnatseach, "for the director," at the head of fifty-five psalms. So this verse shows us harp players who led the music, and it explains a word readers meet constantly in the Psalter.

a: the Levites' leader for the carrying
p: The word massa means "lifting up." It can mean carrying a load, or lifting the voice in song.
b: In Numbers 4 massa means the load the Levites carried, and the ark is the subject here. The King James Version took it as "song," lifting up the voice, since Kenaniah appears among the musicians; many modern versions follow that. It can also mean a prophetic oracle (Isaiah 13:1). The Plain follows the carrying sense, which fits the chapter's concern that the ark be carried properly; 15:27 has the same word.

a: blow the trumpets
p: The trumpets were long straight metal instruments blown by priests. The ram's horn was something else.
b: The chatsotserot were silver trumpets that Moses had made for calling the assembly and for sounding over sacrifices (Numbers 10:1–10). In Chronicles priests usually blow them, though all Israel sounds trumpets in 13:8. The shofar, a ram's horn, is also sounded in this procession (15:28). The trumpets appear on the Arch of Titus in Rome, which shows them carried off from the Temple in AD 70.

a: they sacrificed seven young bulls and seven rams
p: Samuel says David sacrificed an ox and a fat calf after six steps. The scroll 4QSam-a is reported to agree with Chronicles.
b: 2 Samuel 6:13 in the Masoretic text has David sacrifice an ox and a fatling every six steps, or once after six steps. Chronicles has seven bulls and seven rams, offered because God helped the Levites. The Dead Sea scroll 4QSam-a, as reported by its editors, also has seven bulls and seven rams (see the variant at 2 Samuel 6:13). So Chronicles may again follow a Samuel text that differed from ours. Seven bulls and seven rams is a large, full offering (Job 42:8; Ezekiel 45:23).

a: David was wrapped in a robe of fine linen
p: Samuel: David whirled with all his strength. Chronicles: David was wrapped in a robe of fine linen.
b: In Hebrew the two phrases look strangely alike: Samuel's mekharker bekhol-'oz, "whirling with all strength," and Chronicles' mekhurbal bim'il buts, "wrapped in a robe of linen." Many scholars think the Chronicler read or reshaped a damaged phrase in his Samuel scroll. Others think he deliberately dressed David like the Levites, in the linen of Temple musicians (2 Chronicles 5:12), to make him the leader of worship rather than a wild dancer. Chronicles does keep the dancing in 15:29.

a: in her heart she felt contempt for him
p: Chronicles keeps Michal's contempt, but drops the quarrel that follows in Samuel.
b: In 2 Samuel 6:20–23 Michal mocks David, David answers her, and the story ends with her childlessness. Chronicles keeps only this verse, and the line now stands alone. Some take that as proof that the Chronicler assumed his readers knew Samuel. Others think the one verse is enough for his purpose: Saul's daughter, like Saul (13:3), does not share David's joy in the ark. Feminist readers have noted that in both books Michal is never allowed to speak for herself as fully as David does.

a: a loaf of bread, a date cake and a raisin cake
p: The word eshpar appears only here and in Samuel's parallel. Its meaning is a guess.
b: Older versions guessed "a portion of meat" (KJV "a good piece of flesh"), linking it with a word for a share. Many modern versions say "a cake of dates." Samuel has challat lechem, a ring-shaped or round loaf, where Chronicles has kikkar lechem, a loaf. The gift was a festival portion, food for a day of celebration, given to every man and woman.

a: to call him to mind, to give thanks, and to praise
p: The Levites' work is summed up in three verbs: remember, thank, praise.
b: Lehazkir, "to cause to remember," can mean to call on God's name, to remind God, or to commemorate his deeds. The same word is in the titles of Psalms 38 and 70. Lehodot is to give thanks or confess, and lehallel to praise, the root of "hallelujah." The psalm that follows does all three.

a: then Jeiel
p: The first Jeiel is probably the Jaaziel or Aziel of 15:18 and 15:20, miscopied.
b: The list repeats Jeiel at the end, where it belongs (15:18, 21). The first is likely a slip for Jaaziel, who stands in that place in the earlier lists. Names of this kind are easily confused in Hebrew, and no ancient witness settles it.

a: It was on that day that David first gave the task of thanking the LORD to Asaph
p: The Hebrew can be read as David giving Asaph a task, or as David handing him this song.
b: Word for word it says "Then on that day David gave at the head to give thanks to the LORD by the hand of Asaph." The King James Version read it as David delivering "this psalm" to Asaph, and many readers have taken David as its author. The verse does not call it "a psalm of David," and nearly all of it appears in the Book of Psalms without his name (see 16:8). Most scholars think the Chronicler set a known temple song at this moment; traditional readers have often seen David as its first composer or collector.

a: Give thanks to the LORD; call out his name.
t: A psalm made of three psalms
p: 1 Chronicles 16:8–22 is Psalm 105:1–15; 1 Chronicles 16:23–33 is most of Psalm 96; 1 Chronicles 16:34–36 is from Psalm 106.
b: The song joins parts of three psalms. From Psalm 105 it keeps the covenant with Abraham and the promise of the land, and leaves out the exodus and wilderness. From Psalm 96 it keeps the call to all nations to praise the LORD as King. From Psalm 106 it takes the refrain of loyal love, the prayer "gather us from the nations," and the closing blessing. The result fits the Chronicler's readers: a small people, back in the land, among the nations, waiting to be gathered. Most scholars think the Chronicler quoted psalms that already existed; a few think the order went the other way.

a: you seed of Israel, his servant
p: Psalm 105:6 reads "seed of Abraham his servant." Chronicles reads "seed of Israel."
b: Israel here is Jacob, the ancestor of the twelve tribes, as the next line shows. Chronicles likes to call Jacob "Israel" (1:34; 2:1; 29:10, 18), and the change makes the singers' audience, the people of Israel, the direct heirs of the promise. Both readings are old.

a: Keep his covenant in mind for all time
p: Psalm 105:8 says God remembers his covenant. Chronicles calls the people to remember it.
b: The difference is one vowel sound and one letter: zakhar, "he remembered," in the psalm, and zikhru, "remember!", here. In Chronicles the whole first part of the song becomes a call to the people: give thanks, sing, seek, remember. In 16:19 Chronicles also has "when you were few" where the psalm says "when they were few," as if the Levites were speaking straight to the ancestors' descendants.

a: Hands off my anointed ones!
p: Here "anointed ones" means Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, not kings. The verse is often misused.
b: The patriarchs were never anointed with oil, but God set them apart, and Abraham is called a prophet (Genesis 20:7). The plural meshichay shows the word could mean anyone God chose and protected. This is the first use of mashiach, "anointed one," in this part of Chronicles; in later Jewish and Christian use the same word became "Messiah," the coming king (see 17:11–14), but that is not its sense here. Many have quoted this line to shield religious leaders from criticism. In context it is God's warning to foreign kings, such as Pharaoh and Abimelech, who threatened the wandering patriarchs (Genesis 12:17; Genesis 20:3–7).

a: Sing to the LORD, all the earth
p: Chronicles begins Psalm 96 at its second line. The psalm opens "Sing to the LORD a new song."
b: Chronicles starts with the call to all the earth, and it leaves out the psalm's last line about judging the world in righteousness. The section's theme is the LORD as King of every nation, which suited readers who lived as a small province inside the Persian Empire.

a: a nothing-god
p: A pun in Hebrew: the gods (elohim) of the peoples are elilim, "nothings."
b: Elilim sounds like elohim, "gods," but comes from a word meaning weak or worthless (Job 13:4, "worthless physicians"). The prophets and the Law use it for idols (Leviticus 19:4; Isaiah 2:8, 18). The line sets the empty gods against the God who made the heavens.

a: his place is full of strength and joy
p: Psalm 96:6 says "in his sanctuary." Chronicles says "in his place."
b: Psalm 96 sets strength and beauty "in his sanctuary" and calls the peoples to "come into his courts" (96:8). Chronicles has "in his place" and "come into his presence" (16:29). Many scholars think the Chronicler changed the words because the Temple did not yet exist when David's singers first sang. Chronicles also has "joy" (chedvah, a late word, as in Nehemiah 8:10) for the psalm's "beauty."

a: Bow low to the LORD in holy splendor
p: The phrase may describe the worshipers' festive clothes, or God's own holy majesty.
b: Hadrat qodesh has been read as "in holy attire," the clean garments of worshipers, or as "in the splendor of holiness," God's glory. The KJV's "in the beauty of holiness" became famous. Some scholars compare a word in Ugaritic poetry meaning a divine appearance, and translate "when he appears in holiness." All three readings have support.

a: The LORD is King!
p: YHWH malakh can mean "the LORD reigns" or "the LORD has become King."
b: The phrase is the cry of the "kingship psalms" (Psalm 93:1; Psalm 96:10; Psalm 97:1; Psalm 99:1). Sigmund Mowinckel argued that they were sung at a yearly festival celebrating God's enthronement; many scholars now doubt the festival but agree the psalms proclaim God's rule over all nations. In Psalm 96 the cry comes at verse 10; Chronicles moves it into the call for heaven and earth to rejoice.

a: because he is coming to judge the earth
p: Psalm 96 ends with the LORD coming to judge the world. Chronicles keeps the coming and drops the last line.
b: Psalm 96:13 says twice that the LORD comes, and adds that he will judge the world with righteousness and the peoples with his faithfulness. Chronicles keeps one "coming" and stops. Jewish readers have heard in the psalm the hope of God's kingdom on earth; Christians have read it as pointing to Christ's return (Acts 17:31). The trees shouting for joy appear also in Isaiah 55:12.

a: his loyal love is forever
p: The refrain of God's lasting loyal love is the most repeated song line in Chronicles.
b: The refrain sounds when the ark enters the Temple and the glory fills it (2 Chronicles 5:13), when fire falls on the altar (2 Chronicles 7:3, 6), before Jehoshaphat's battle (2 Chronicles 20:21), and when the returned exiles lay the new Temple's foundation (Ezra 3:11). Psalm 136 repeats it in every verse. Hesed is God's faithful, covenant-keeping love; this site renders it "loyal love."

a: Gather us and pull us out from the nations
t: An exiles' prayer in David's day
p: David's singers pray to be gathered from the nations, centuries before the exile.
b: The line comes from Psalm 106:47, the prayer of scattered Israel. In David's day the people were not scattered. Critical scholars see the Chronicler's own time showing through: his readers, many of whose relatives still lived in Babylon and Egypt, sang this prayer. Traditional readers have read it as prophetic, or as a general cry for rescue from enemies. Chronicles adds "God who rescues us" and "pull us out," which strengthen the plea.

a: And the whole people said, "Amen!" and gave praise to the LORD.
t: The end of Book Four of the Psalms
p: Psalm 106:48 is the blessing that closes Book Four of Psalms. Chronicles quotes it, and turns it into a story.
b: The Psalter is divided into five books, each ending with a blessing (Psalm 41:13; Psalm 72:19; Psalm 89:52; Psalm 106:48). Psalm 106:48 ends "Let all the people say, 'Amen.' Hallelujah!" Chronicles reports it as something that happened: the people said Amen and praised the LORD. Many scholars argue that, if Chronicles is quoting the psalm, the closing blessing of Book Four already existed in its day, which helps date the shaping of the Psalter. Others think the blessing was a liturgical response used in many places.

a: Obed-edom son of Jedithun
p: Here the Hebrew spells the name Jedithun. In 16:41–42 it is Jeduthun.
b: The Plain keeps the spelling of this verse. Readers differ on who this is. Some take him as the singer Jeduthun of 16:41, which would make this Obed-edom a singer's son. Others think he is a different man, since Obed-edom the gatekeeper belongs to a Korahite family in 26:1–8. Chronicles also seems to know more than one Obed-edom (compare 15:18, 15:21 and 15:24).

a: before the LORD's tabernacle at the high place that was in Gibeon
p: Chronicles places Moses' tabernacle and altar at Gibeon in David's time.
b: The tabernacle was last at Shiloh (1 Samuel 1–4) and perhaps Nob (1 Samuel 21). Samuel and Kings never say it moved to Gibeon, but 1 Kings 3:4 calls Gibeon "the great high place" where Solomon sacrificed. Chronicles explains that the old tent was there (21:29; 2 Chronicles 1:3–6). Some scholars take this as an old memory; others see the Chronicler explaining why Solomon worshiped at a high place, which Kings normally condemns. Either way, it lets Chronicles show regular lawful sacrifice continuing while the ark waited in its tent.

a: morning and evening
p: The law required a burnt offering every morning and every evening.
b: The regular burnt offering, the tamid, was a lamb offered at dawn and another at dusk, with flour, oil and wine (Exodus 29:38–42; Numbers 28:3–8). Chronicles insists it never stopped, even while the ark was apart from the altar. In later Jewish practice the morning and afternoon prayers took the place of these offerings.

a: the LORD's law
p: The Hebrew word torah means "instruction" or "teaching" more than a legal code.
b: Torah comes from a verb meaning "to point the way, to teach." In Chronicles it usually means the written instruction of Moses, here the rules for the daily offering (Numbers 28:3–8). For Jewish readers the word names the five books of Moses, and more broadly all of God's teaching.

a: Heman and Jeduthun
p: Jeduthun leads the singers at Gibeon. His name is in three psalm titles.
b: Psalms 39, 62 and 77 mention Jeduthun in their headings. In 25:1–6 his sons are among the Temple musicians, and 2 Chronicles 35:15 calls him "the king's visionary." Because Jeduthun takes the place that Ethan holds in 1 Chronicles 15:17, many scholars think the two names belong to one man or one family. So the singers were split between the two sanctuaries: Asaph before the ark in Jerusalem, Heman and Jeduthun at the altar in Gibeon.
r: Psalm 39; Psalm 62; Psalm 77; 1 Chronicles 25:1–6; 2 Chronicles 35:15; 1 Chronicles 15:17

a: David had made his home in his house.
p: Samuel adds that the LORD had given David rest from all his enemies. Chronicles leaves it out.
b: In 2 Samuel 7:1 the scene opens with rest from every enemy. Chronicles drops those words, and the reason becomes clear later. David will tell Solomon that God refused him because he had shed much blood and fought great wars (22:8), and promised a son who would be a man of rest (22:9). In Chronicles, rest belongs to Solomon, whose name sounds like shalom, "peace." So the Temple must wait for him. Chapters 18–20, with their wars, follow at once.

a: the ark of the LORD's covenant is under curtains
p: The ark lived inside a tent made of long woven panels, the yeri'ot.
b: The tabernacle was made of ten curtains of fine linen and eleven of goats' hair (Exodus 26:1–13). David's tent for the ark (15:1) was probably of the same kind. The contrast is between a king's cedar palace and God's cloth tent. Chronicles calls it "the ark of the LORD's covenant," its fuller title, where Samuel says "God's ark."

a: It is not you who will build the house for me to live in.
p: In Samuel God asks, "Is it you who will build me a house?" Chronicles says flatly, "Not you."
b: Samuel's question can be read as a refusal or as a gentle challenge, and readers have debated whether God objected to a temple at all. Chronicles removes the doubt: God wants a house, but David is not the one to build it, and it is "the house," the Temple everyone knew. The same point is made in 22:8 and 28:3, where the reason is given: David was a man of war.

a: from tent to tent, and from one tabernacle to another
p: The Hebrew is cut short: "from tent to tent and from tabernacle." The rest of the phrase seems lost.
b: The natural pattern would be "from tabernacle to tabernacle," and a copyist could easily lose the repeated word. Samuel has "I have walked about in a tent, in a tabernacle" (2 Samuel 7:6). Chronicles' version stresses movement: the ark had been at Gilgal, Shiloh, Kiriath-jearim and now Jerusalem. The Plain supplies the missing words.

a: any of Israel's judges
p: Chronicles reads "judges" where Samuel's Hebrew has "tribes." The two words differ by one letter.
b: "Judges" (shofte) fits the next words, "the ones I ordered to shepherd my people," better than "tribes" (shivte), and many modern translations of Samuel adopt the Chronicles reading. This site's 2 Samuel keeps "tribes" and shows "judges" as a variant there. 17:10 also mentions the judges.

a: it is a house that the LORD will build for you
p: "House" means a temple and a dynasty. Chronicles uses "build" where Samuel says "make."
b: In Hebrew "build" (banah) and "son" (ben) sound alike, and the Bible plays on the pair: a man's house is "built" by his sons (Genesis 16:2; Ruth 4:11). Samuel says the LORD will "make" David a house; Chronicles says "build," which matches David's wish to "build" God a house (17:4, 12). David will not build God's house; God will build David's, and David's son will build God's. The Hebrew puts "a house" first for emphasis.

a: one who will come from among your sons
p: Samuel says "one who comes from your own body." Chronicles says "one of your sons," pointing to Solomon.
b: In Samuel the promise is open: any descendant could be meant, and in 2 Samuel 7:14 the son may sin and be punished. Chronicles narrows the focus to one son, and later names him as Solomon (22:9). Many scholars think Chronicles reads the promise as fulfilled in two steps, a lasting dynasty and a chosen son who builds the Temple. The phrase "go to join your ancestors" also replaces Samuel's "lie down with your ancestors"; both mean death.

a: I will be a father to him, and he will be a son to me.
p: The New Testament quotes this line for Jesus. Chronicles quotes it for Solomon three times.
b: Hebrews 1:5 quotes these words, with Psalm 2:7, to show the Son is greater than the angels; Paul applies them to all believers in 2 Corinthians 6:18. In Chronicles the promise returns in 22:10 and 28:6, both times about Solomon. Psalm 89:26–27 expands it: the king will call God "my Father." In the ancient Near East kings were often called sons of a god; in Israel the language expressed a covenant bond, not divine birth. Christians read it as fulfilled fully in Christ.

a: I will not take my loyal love away from him
p: Samuel adds, "If he does wrong, I will correct him with a rod." Chronicles leaves that out.
b: In 2 Samuel 7:14 God expects the son to sin and promises discipline, not rejection. Chronicles drops the warning. Its Solomon never sins: no foreign wives lead him to idols and no kingdom is torn away in its account of his reign, though Pharaoh's daughter is mentioned (2 Chronicles 8:11; compare 1 Kings 11 with 2 Chronicles 9). Many scholars see Chronicles idealizing Solomon as the perfect Temple builder. Others note that Chronicles still makes the promise conditional elsewhere (28:7, 9), so it has not removed the warning, only moved it. Saul is not named here either, only "the one who was before you."

a: I will make him stand in my house and in my kingdom
p: Samuel: "your house and your kingdom." Chronicles: "my house and my kingdom." The kingdom is God's.
b: This is the most important change in the chapter. In Samuel the promise is to David's dynasty. In Chronicles the son is placed in God's house (the Temple, and God's own household) and in God's kingdom. Later Solomon sits on the LORD's throne (29:23), and Abijah calls Judah the LORD's kingdom in the hands of David's sons (2 Chronicles 13:8). For readers with no king, this meant the kingdom had not ended: it was always God's. Jewish readers have seen here the hope of the Messiah's kingdom; Christians hear it in the angel's words that Jesus will reign over the house of Jacob forever (Luke 1:32–33).
r: 2 Samuel 7:16; 1 Chronicles 28:5; 1 Chronicles 29:11; 1 Chronicles 29:23; 2 Chronicles 13:8; Luke 1:32–33

a: LORD God, who am I?
p: Samuel's prayer says Adonai YHWH, "Lord GOD." Chronicles says YHWH Elohim, "LORD God."
b: Throughout David's prayer, Samuel uses Adonai YHWH seven times. Chronicles uses YHWH Elohim or simply YHWH or Elohim. This site renders YHWH Elohim as "LORD God" and Adonai YHWH as "Lord GOD," so the difference stays visible. Chronicles never uses the title Adonai YHWH at all; scholars connect this with its general style rather than a theological objection.

a: you have seen me as one would see a man of high rank
p: Both Samuel and Chronicles are hard here, and they are hard in different ways.
b: Samuel says "and this is the law (torah) of humankind." Chronicles reads "you have seen me like the tor of the man, the going up." Tor may mean a rank or a turn, and hamma'alah "the one going up" or "on high." Translations give: "you regard me as a man of high degree" (KJV), "you have shown me future generations," or, with small emendations, "you have looked on me as a man going up." The Plain follows the first sense. Every reading keeps David's wonder that God should honor him.
orig: וּרְאִיתַנִי כְּתוֹר הָאָדָם הַמַּעֲלָה (ure'itani ketor ha'adam hamma'alah)

a: driving out nations ahead of your people
p: Samuel's line is tangled. Chronicles reads "by driving out nations."
b: In 2 Samuel 7:23 the Masoretic text says God redeemed Israel "from Egypt, from nations and their gods," and the Greek says "driving out nations and their tents." Chronicles has legaresh, "to drive out," which many think was also in the Hebrew behind the Greek. See the variant at 2 Samuel 7:23.

a: and it stays blessed forever
p: Samuel ends with a request. Chronicles ends with a confident statement: God has blessed.
b: In 2 Samuel 7:29 David asks God to be willing to bless his house, and hopes "your blessing will rest on your servant's house." Chronicles uses past tenses: "you have been willing," "you have blessed it." The prayer ends on certainty. For a community whose kings were gone, Chronicles insists the blessing had already been given and could not be taken back.

a: Some time later
p: Samuel puts David's kindness to Mephibosheth between this chapter and the next. Chronicles skips it.
b: 2 Samuel 9 tells how David found Jonathan's lame son Mephibosheth and gave him a place at the king's table. Chronicles leaves out that chapter, as it leaves out Saul's house in general after chapter 10, though it gives Mephibosheth's line under the name Merib-baal (8:34; 9:40). The wars of 2 Samuel 8 and 10 follow one after the other.

a: Gath and its villages
p: Samuel's puzzling "Metheg-ammah" becomes "Gath and its villages" in Chronicles.
b: Metheg-ha'ammah in 2 Samuel 8:1 may mean "the bridle of the mother city," that is, control of the chief city. Chronicles names that city, Gath, and its "daughters," the Hebrew way of saying its surrounding villages. Most scholars think Chronicles is explaining an old phrase rather than following a different text. Gath was the home of Goliath and of Achish, David's former protector.
orig: גַּת וּבְנֹתֶיהָ (Gat uvenoteha), 'Gath and her daughters'

a: He beat Moab too.
p: Chronicles leaves out Samuel's grim scene of Moabite prisoners killed by measured rows.
b: In 2 Samuel 8:2 David makes the Moabites lie down and measures off two lines for death and one for life. Chronicles keeps only the victory and the tribute. Some think it softened a harsh deed; others note that Chronicles keeps plenty of violence (20:3), and simply shortened the account. Samuel gives no reason for the harshness either, though David had once trusted his parents to Moab's king (1 Samuel 22:3–4).

a: to set up his victory marker by the Euphrates River
p: Samuel says he went to "restore his hand"; Chronicles, to "set up his hand." A hand can mean a monument.
b: The Hebrew word yad, "hand," also means a memorial stone: Saul set up a yad at Carmel (1 Samuel 15:12), and Absalom's monument was "Absalom's hand" (2 Samuel 18:18). Samuel's lehashiv and Chronicles' lehatsiv differ by one letter. Either way the sentence is unclear about whether David or Hadadezer was marching toward the Euphrates. Kings of the time set up victory stelae at the edges of their power.

a: a thousand chariots, seven thousand horsemen
p: Chronicles has a thousand chariots and seven thousand horsemen. So do the Greek of Samuel and 4QSam-a.
b: The Hebrew (Masoretic) text of 2 Samuel 8:4 has only "one thousand seven hundred horsemen," and it never mentions the chariots that David then hamstrings. Chronicles, the Greek of Samuel and the Dead Sea scroll 4QSam-a read "a thousand chariots and seven thousand horsemen." This site's 2 Samuel follows that reading, so the two books now match (see the variant at 2 Samuel 8:4).

a: David stationed troops in Aram of Damascus
p: The Hebrew of Chronicles says only that David "put" in Aram; the word "garrisons" is missing.
b: Samuel has netsivim, "garrisons" or "governors." Chronicles has the verb without its object, most likely because a copyist dropped the word. Every translation supplies it from Samuel and from 18:13, where Chronicles does have it.

a: It was what Solomon used to make the bronze Sea, the pillars
p: Chronicles adds that the captured bronze went into Solomon's Temple. The Greek of Samuel has a similar note.
b: The bronze Sea was the huge basin in the Temple court, and the pillars were Jachin and Boaz at its entrance (1 Kings 7:15–26; 2 Chronicles 4:2–5). The Greek of 2 Samuel 8:8 has a similar sentence, so the note was not simply the Chronicler's invention; it may have stood in some Samuel texts (see the variant at 2 Samuel 8:8). It fits Chronicles' picture of David's whole reign, even his wars, as preparation for the Temple (22:3, 14).

a: Tibhath and Cun
p: Samuel names the towns Betah and Berothai. Their locations in the Beqaa Valley are uncertain.
b: Tibhath may be the Tebah of Genesis 22:24 (an Aramean clan name), and Samuel's "Betah" looks like the same name with letters reversed. Cun has sometimes been placed near Baalbek in Lebanon; Berothai may be the Berothah of Ezekiel 47:16. The two books may be using different names for the same towns.

a: his son Hadoram
p: Samuel calls Tou's son Joram, "the LORD is exalted." Chronicles calls him Hadoram, "Hadad is exalted."
b: Hadad was the storm god of the Arameans, so Hadoram is the more natural name for a prince of Hamath. Some think the prince took an Israelite name as a sign of friendship; others think a scribe of Samuel changed an unfamiliar name to a familiar one. The king's name is also spelled differently: Toi in Samuel, Tou here.

a: The royal scribe was Shavsha.
p: David's scribe has a different name in each list. It may be a foreign name or title.
b: 2 Samuel 8:17 calls him Seraiah, 2 Samuel 20:25 Sheva, and 1 Kings 4:3 names Solomon's scribes as "sons of Shisha." Some scholars think the name comes from an Egyptian title for a royal letter writer, since Israel's first royal officials may have copied Egyptian models. Others think the forms are simply copying variants of one Hebrew name.

a: David's sons were first in rank beside the king
p: Samuel says David's sons "served as priests." Chronicles says they were first beside the king.
b: In 2 Samuel 8:18 David's sons are kohanim, "priests." For Chronicles only Aaron's descendants could be priests, so sons of Judah could not have been. It gives instead what it took the title to mean: chief officials at the king's side. The Aramaic Targum of Samuel likewise makes them chiefs rather than priests. Scholars debate whether early Israel allowed royal princes a priestly role (compare 2 Samuel 20:26) or whether "priest" had a wider sense then.

a: Nahash, the Ammonites' king, died
p: Chronicles names the king, Nahash. Samuel says only "the Ammonite king."
b: A Nahash besieged Jabesh-gilead at the start of Saul's reign (1 Samuel 11). If this is the same man, he reigned a long time, and he may have helped David as an enemy of Saul. His son Shobi later brought supplies to David in exile (2 Samuel 17:27). David's "loyal love" toward Hanun repays that old friendship.

a: a thousand talents of silver
p: A talent weighed about 75 pounds. A thousand talents was some 37 tons of silver.
b: Samuel does not give the price; Chronicles does. The sum is enormous, as much as Menahem of Israel later paid the king of Assyria to keep his throne (2 Kings 15:19). It shows how afraid Ammon was after its insult to David.

a: Aram-naharaim, Aram-maacah and Zobah
p: Chronicles' list of allies differs from Samuel's and reaches as far as the Euphrates.
b: Samuel lists Beth-rehob, Zobah, Maacah and Tob (2 Samuel 10:6). Chronicles has Aram-naharaim, "Aram of the two rivers," in upper Mesopotamia, the homeland of Abraham's kin (Genesis 24:10), along with Maacah and Zobah. The title of Psalm 60 also mentions Aram-naharaim and Aram-zobah together. Hadadezer's later call to Arameans "beyond the River" (19:16) shows his reach did extend that far.

a: thirty-two thousand chariots
p: Samuel counts 33,000 hired men. Chronicles counts 32,000 chariots, a number far beyond any known army.
b: Samuel's total, 20,000 foot soldiers, 1,000 from Maacah and 12,000 from Tob, is 33,000 men. Chronicles has 32,000 rekhev, plus Maacah's troops. For comparison, at the battle of Qarqar in 853 BC an Assyrian inscription credits the whole western alliance with fewer than 4,000 chariots. Some scholars think rekhev here means "chariotry" in a broad sense, the hired army; others think the number was distorted in copying, or that the Chronicler, as often, gives a large round figure.

a: camped facing Medeba
p: Medeba was in Moab, south of Ammon. It is an odd place to camp for a battle at Rabbah.
