b: Medeba stood on the plateau east of the Dead Sea (Numbers 21:30; Joshua 13:9), and the Moabite king Mesha later claimed it on his stone inscription. Rabbah, the Ammonite capital, was about twenty miles north. Some scholars suggest the Hebrew once read "the waters of Rabbah" (compare "the water city," 2 Samuel 12:27); others think the Arameans did gather to the south before marching north.

a: But David was staying in Jerusalem.
p: Here Samuel tells of Bathsheba and Uriah. Chronicles goes straight on to the fall of Rabbah.
b: In Samuel this sentence leads into David's sin with Bathsheba, Uriah's murder, Nathan's rebuke and the child's death (2 Samuel 11:2–12:25). Chronicles skips all of it, and also Joab's message calling David to Rabbah (2 Samuel 12:27–29), so David's sudden appearance there in 20:2 is unexplained. Why the silence? 1. Chronicles idealizes David as a flawless founder (Wellhausen and many since). 2. Chronicles assumes its readers know Samuel, as the gap in 20:1–2 itself shows, and tells only what serves its theme (Japhet, Williamson). 3. Chronicles tells David's reign as the story of the Temple's founder; the private sins of his family do not bear on that, while the sin of the census does, and Chronicles tells it in full (chapter 21). Readers can hold these views together.

a: at the season when kings march out
p: Chronicles spells "kings" plainly. In Samuel's written text the word looks like "messengers."
b: In 2 Samuel 11:1 the consonants read hammal'akhim, "the messengers," and the Masoretes marked it to be read hammelakhim, "the kings." Chronicles has "kings" in its text, which supports the read form. Spring, after the rains, was the season for campaigns.

a: a talent of gold
t: A crown too heavy to wear?
p: A talent was about 75 pounds (34 kg). Readers have long asked how anyone wore it.
b: The Talmud (Avodah Zarah 44a) already raises the question. Some think the crown belonged to the statue of Milcom, the Ammonite god, since "their king" (malkam) can be read as Milcom (see the variant at 2 Samuel 12:30); David then wore only the precious stone, or wore the crown briefly. Others think the weight is that of the whole treasure taken with the crown. Chronicles adds that David "found" its weight, perhaps by weighing it.

a: at Gezer
p: Samuel places this battle at Gob, an unknown place. Chronicles says Gezer.
b: Gob appears only in 2 Samuel 21:18–19 and is otherwise unknown; Gezer was a well-known city on the border of Philistine country, already named in 1 Chronicles 14:16. Some think Chronicles replaced an obscure name with a known one; others think "Gob" in Samuel is a copying error. Chronicles also omits the place in the next verse.

a: one of the offspring of the Rephaim
p: Samuel says "born to the Rapha." Chronicles says "of the Rephaim," the name of the ancient giants.
b: The Rephaim were a legendary tall people of Canaan (Deuteronomy 2:11, 20; Deuteronomy 3:11). "Rapha" in 20:6 and 20:8 may be an ancestor's name, the giants' clan, or, as some scholars suggest, a title for a warrior group devoted to a god. In Ugaritic texts the rpum are honored dead kings. Chronicles reads the Philistine champions as descendants of the old giants, the same race the spies had feared (Numbers 13:33).
r: 2 Samuel 21:18; Deuteronomy 2:11; Deuteronomy 3:11; Numbers 13:33; 1 Chronicles 20:6; 1 Chronicles 20:8

a: Some time later
p: Between 20:3 and 20:4 Chronicles passes over eight chapters of Samuel.
b: 2 Samuel 13–20 tells of Amnon and Tamar, Absalom's murder of Amnon, his revolt and death, and Sheba's rebellion. Chronicles skips all of it and goes straight to the giant stories of 2 Samuel 21:18–22. For three ways of reading this silence, see the book's opening page, "What Chronicles leaves out," and the note on 20:1.

a: Elhanan son of Jair struck down Lahmi the brother of Goliath the Gittite
p: 2 Samuel 21:19 says Elhanan killed Goliath. Chronicles says he killed Goliath's brother Lahmi.
b: The Hebrew of the two verses is close: Samuel's beit hallachmi et golyat, "the Bethlehemite... Goliath," and Chronicles' et-lachmi achi golyat, "Lahmi the brother of Goliath." 1. Chronicles keeps the original, and Samuel's text was damaged (many conservative scholars). 2. Samuel keeps the original: an Elhanan killed a giant named Goliath, and the famous name later attached to David's victory; Chronicles then read the hard text so as to agree with 1 Samuel 17 (many critical scholars, such as McCarter). 3. Jewish tradition (the Targum on Samuel) took Elhanan to be another name for David. Samuel's "Jaare-oregim" also seems to borrow "weavers" (oregim) from the end of the verse; Chronicles' "Jair" is probably right.

a: These had been born to the Rapha in Gath.
p: Samuel's list starts with a giant who nearly kills an exhausted David. Chronicles leaves him out.
b: In 2 Samuel 21:15–17 David grows weary in battle, Ishbi-benob plans to kill him, Abishai saves him, and David's men swear he will never fight with them again. Chronicles' list begins with the second giant, and so Samuel's "these four" becomes "these." Some see Chronicles sparing David an undignified moment; others think the Chronicler began at a natural break, since 20:4 follows 2 Samuel 21:18 closely. The chapter, and this part of David's story, ends with victory: David and his servants brought them down.
